Bielsko-Biała (Biała) Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Bielsko-Biała, Poland

Demolished. Biała (merged into Bielsko-Biała in 1951) saw its first Jewish settlers in the late 17th century, with population reaching 20% by 1752 before a 1765 court-ordered expulsion barred Jews until 1848; growth resumed afterward, reaching 3,942 residents by 1938. This cemetery, established in 1849 (initially leased, purchased outright in 1902), held about 2,000 burials by 1955. Wartime brought ghettoization and 1942-43 Auschwitz-Birkenau deportations, and postwar Jewish emigration (especially after 1968's antisemitic campaigns) left the community nearly extinguished by the 1970s. The cemetery itself was abandoned in 1956 and designated for industrial use; a 1958 fittings factory took over its western section, requiring the first exhumations. Despite Jewish protests and legal challenges, authorities liquidated the cemetery fully in 1966 for a sporting-goods factory expansion, giving families just two weeks to arrange exhumations - only about 130 graves were relocated at factory expense, with the remaining 1,500 moved to a shared grave. About one-third of surviving tombstones (180) were relocated to the Bielsko cemetery on Cieszyńska Street; the rest were stolen or repurposed for construction, including hardening a streambed and factory grounds. As of 2021, the site's future remained uncertain, with a 2017 city development plan permitting housing construction on the former cemetery grounds.
